title: Why is Snowpiercer so good? I can't put my finger on it.

Snowpiercer says something that resonates in a lot of us: there are people that control and define society, and the oppressed who wish to break the chains.


It's not different from, say, Star Wars in it's message. Or even the New Testament. It's a common story.


And Chris Evans is damn good in it.

I think that's just Bong Joon-ho's style.

I agree, Snowpiercer is a good film, it's well paced and I enjoy the style. The action scenes are intense but not too much. More than anything though, I appreciate the commentary on our modern world and the unique dystopia.

That said, I think Parasite (2019) and Okja (2017) are better films with similar themes. If you haven't seen them yet, you should check them out. Same director, just a bit better executed.

The answer is Bong Joon-ho. I've noticed this across almost all of his films, especially his non-English ones Memories of Murder, Mother, and Parasite. 

My main theory being he's a master of restricted information. He never tells the viewer everything and almost all of his movies feel like a mystery that the viewer is watching unfold, even if the movie isn't a mystery movie. His movies always seem to build up to something and we usually don't know what that something is. The motto for all his movies is basically "things aren't what they seem," whether it's post-apocalyptic fantasy or a serial killer manhunt, and the audience FEELS that. Mystery is so strong, it almost feels sinister. Even a simple house in Parasite holds secrets. The boy talks about a figure coming out of the basement, something that isn't even mentioned until much later. But we heard it, and it makes us feel like there's something more under the surface, even if it's just subconscious. He didn't have to make it like that, but that's him, that's his touch. It's why his movies are so good on a second viewing, you notice so many clues subtly placed that you didn't even know you noticed the first time. 

They're snappy and intentional in the way the plot is set up and unfolds, very little dead weight. His directing style is incredibly immersive, whether it be sucking you into a grungy police office trying to catch a serial killer or a post-apocalyptic future. His movies give off "this is what movies should feel like" more than most other films and most don't really know why, but they feel it. He also writes his movies and his scripts share the same quality, even if you just read them. The reason being he masterfully knows how to utilize restricted information and gradually nudge the viewer closer to a truth, and the truth is almost always a plot twist. They're also unique to a lot of people in that they don't follow Western conventions of storytelling. With Snowpiercer this is very captivating because it's an English action movie with a Western superstar (very intentional) to play with expectations. 

When you combine his style of restricted information with the rest of his storytelling abilities (themes, character writing, pacing, Hitchcockian scenes, magical and surreal world-building), you get movies that truly know what the fuck they're doing at every second. I have no doubt he's gonna do it again too.

I thought the social critique was a bit heavy-handed (I’m not as huge on Squid Game as many people are for the same reason) but the movie really shined to me in the fact that it had a unique premise and it executed that fantastically. The fact that the movie took itself seriously too despite the wild premise is also an underrated reason why it’s as good as it is. 

On that last point, I think it’s why the modern Planet of the Apes movies have been as good as they are. The premise is a little wacky but they always take the movie seriously and it never falls into the trap of making fun of itself, like something like an MCU movie often does.

One thing that stood out to me after not seeing it for a couple of years is how genuinely disturbing it is. It’s sci-fi and has a pretty insane premise, but the authoritarianism it depicts feels really realistic (and brutal). I think the world building is fantastic. And the dismemberment scene is one of the most horrific movies scenes I’ve ever seen.

I think the heavy handed social critique might actually be the key to nailing that tone you're talking about. It's the Verhoeven school of making fun movies.
This is just my obligatory comment where I say Memories of Murder is his best film.
I mean if you’re going to homage two dystopian sci fi movies, you really can’t do better.

The heavy handedness was to make the ending point crystal clear: Class warfare will continue to repeat itself in cycles because the ruling class will engage endlessly in recuperation.


What's the answer to that problem? Blow the whole system up and start over. Loved it.
Memories of Murder is so freaking good.  Mother is a close second for me.  He really doesn’t have an outright “bad” film.
Best ending for sure.
Memories of murder might just be one of my favorite movies of all time. It's just so perfect

Wow, love this write up. Such a part of his language that he shares with Kubrick despite their wildly different styles - is that you know things aren't what they seem, and there's a darker truth lurking beneath. It makes his movies into their own worlds where you want to turn everything over.
It's one of those movies that I just appreciate more and more with every watch. It really is so fantastic.

i absolutely agree. in fact, i think it's the best korean movie ever made. 

i was thinking about it just this morning for whatever reason, not having seen it for so long. time for a rewatch

This is still my most disappointing film ever, i thought it'd be a serious moody thoughtful sci fi about people trafficking in space, not a comic book film. I'd watched Memories of Murder and Mother the year before, so instant big fan of the director. 

I hated its tone and by the end enjoyed some of the action but it was all a waste of potential for me.
